summary: Defines an RTCP Extended Report block that reports how many bytes were discarded from the de-jitter buffer after being received successfully. This helps measure the quality of real-time media sessions.

eli5.summary: A video call keeps a small waiting area to smooth out late pieces. Sometimes it has to throw some pieces away. This report tells how much was thrown away.

questions: what is rtcp xr bytes discarded
what is rtcp xr block type 26
what does the early bit mean in rtcp xr
subtitle: A small RTCP report that tells a media sender exactly how many payload bytes the receiver threw away from its de-jitter buffer.

tldr.problem: Existing RTCP reports can count discarded packets, but none lets a receiver say precisely how many RTP payload bytes it discarded after receiving them successfully.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7243 defines an RTCP Extended Report block (block type 26) carrying a 32-bit count of discarded RTP payload bytes, either per reporting interval or since the session began, with an Early bit to separate early from late discards.
tldr.outcome: A sender can use the count, for example to calculate goodput for congestion control. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 7243 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the Bytes Discarded Report Block for RTCP XR.

sections.title: Why Count Discarded Bytes
sections.content:
RTP carries real-time media such as audio and video, and RTCP sends periodic feedback about the streams. A receiver keeps a de-jitter buffer to smooth out uneven packet arrival. A packet that was received but dropped from that buffer because it arrived too early to buffer or too late to play is called discarded. RFC 3611 already defines a discard rate for such packets.

Other extensions count discarded packets (RFC 7002), report gaps and bursts of discards (RFC 7003), or run-length encode which packets were discarded (RFC 7097). None of them lets a receiver report precisely the number of RTP payload bytes discarded. Deriving it from frequent packet-count reports would need an unduly high amount of reporting, and the run-length approach needs a map of sequence numbers and packet sizes plus extra overhead.

This document therefore defines one XR block that reports the number of payload bytes discarded, per interval or for the whole session.
sections.eli5: Other reports say how many pieces were thrown away, but not how big they were. This report adds the size, so the sender knows how much was really lost.

sections.title: The Bytes Discarded Report Block
sections.content:
The block is three 32-bit words. The first word holds the block type BT=26, the two-bit Interval Metric flag (I), the Early bit (E), five reserved bits and a block length that MUST be 2. The second word is the SSRC of the source. The third is a 32-bit unsigned count of RTP payload bytes discarded.

The I flag says what period the count covers. I=10 means the most recent interval between successive reports. I=11 means the cumulative total since the start of the session. The metric MUST NOT be reported as a sampled metric (I=01). The value I=00 is reserved, MUST NOT be sent, and MUST be discarded when received.

The E bit is 1 when the bytes were discarded for early arrival and 0 when they were discarded for late arrival. To report both, two blocks MUST be included. Duplicate packets that are received and discarded are ignored and not reported.

The count is the RTP payload size of every discarded packet. It ignores RTP header extensions and padding. A discarded packet counts in the interval in which it was discarded, not the one in which it was expected. A receiver MUST set reserved bits to zero and ignore them, and a block whose length is not 2 MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: The report is a short note with a few boxes to fill in: which stream, whether the pieces came too early or too late, and a number for how many bytes were tossed out.

sections.title: How Receivers and Senders Use It
sections.content:
The receiver MAY send Bytes Discarded reports with its regularly scheduled RTCP packets or in immediate or early feedback packets as described in RFC 4585. When and how often to report is up to the receiver, although it is RECOMMENDED that a receiver signal bytes discarded using this method. Reporting intervals are synchronized when several metrics share one RTCP packet, so a receiver may also add a Discarded Packets or Discard RLE block to help the sender match bytes to packets. If every packet in a period was discarded, the receiver MAY use the Discarded Packets block instead.

Without a Measurement Information Block (RFC 6776), the report MUST travel in a compound RTCP packet together with a Receiver Report. If it follows a Measurement Information Block, the I flag refers to that block's measurement duration.

The sender MUST be prepared to operate with no such reports and cannot count on a regular pattern. If it receives other RTCP reports, no Bytes Discarded block, and knows the receiver supports the block, it MAY assume no packets were discarded. The sender SHOULD accept the block only in a compound receiver report or after a Measurement Information Block, and MUST ignore it otherwise.
sections.eli5: The receiver decides when to send the note. The sender must not rely on getting it, but if the receiver is known to send these notes and none arrives, the sender can guess that nothing was thrown away.

sections.title: Signaling Support with SDP
sections.content:
Participants MAY announce support in SDP or just use the block without prior signaling. For signaling, the rtcp-xr attribute from RFC 3611 MUST be used. This document adds one new xr-format parameter, discard-bytes, written in ABNF as xr-discard-bytes = "discard-bytes".

In an offer/answer exchange, the rule from RFC 3611 for unilateral rtcp-xr parameters applies.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side can say, in a short written note, that it understands this kind of report. It can also just start sending it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The block gives no per-packet statistics, so the confidentiality risk described in RFC 3611 does not apply. Still, detailed error information can leak. If an attacker injects a packet with a stale timestamp and the receiver reports the same number of discarded bytes as that payload, the attacker learns that no security processing was done on it. If no report comes back, the attacker can assume security processing took place.

Where security matters, implementers should follow RFC 7202 and apply encryption and authentication to the block, for example with the AVPF profile together with Secure RTP (the SAVPF combination in RFC 5124). Other options are documented in RFC 7201.

A sender that uses the report for congestion control, typically to calculate goodput, can be attacked: an attacker MAY drive the endpoint to lower its sending rate and under-use the link. Senders should choose suitable security measures. The security considerations of RFC 3550, RFC 3611 and RFC 4585 also apply.
sections.eli5: A sneaky listener could learn things from whether a note comes back, and could lie to make a sender slow down. Locking the messages with encryption helps stop that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document registers block type 26 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry, with the name BDR (Bytes Discarded Report). It also registers the SDP parameter discard-bytes in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry. The contact for both registrations is the RAI Area Directors.

Appendix A describes the metric using the template from RFC 6390: the metric is the total number of RTP payload bytes discarded over the period the report covers.
sections.eli5: The number 26 and the word discard-bytes were written in an official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: 1 for early-arrival discards, 0 for late-arrival discards.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: SSRC of source
fields.desc: The source the report relates to.

fields.name: Number of RTP payload bytes discarded
fields.desc: Unsigned count of discarded payload bytes.

viz.caption: VALUES OF THE INTERVAL METRIC FLAG (I)

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: MUST NOT be sent; MUST be discarded when received.

items.label: Sampled
items.desc: MUST NOT be used for this metric.

items.label: Interval
items.desc: Bytes discarded in the most recent reporting interval.

items.label: Cumulative
items.desc: Bytes discarded since the start of the session.
